correctness.rationale: For even n, central inversion interchanges the two boundary arcs. For odd n=2k+1, normalization to unit circumradius and reduction to 0<=alpha<=pi/n identify the exact two intersected edges. Elementary intersection geometry gives u=t/(sin(2beta)+(1-cos(2beta))t) and v=(1+t*cot(beta))/2. The shorter arc has (n/2-u+v-1/2) edge lengths; their difference simplifies exactly to tan(alpha)tan(beta-alpha)/2. Maximization by the increasing function (cos(2alpha-beta)-cos(beta))/(cos(2alpha-beta)+cos(beta)) gives the unique sector extremum at alpha=beta/2. Sector symmetry, parity, endpoint conditions, and the n^-3 expansion are proved analytically. Separate geometric boundary-enumeration numerical checks for n=3,...,37 and exact rational identity spot checks pass, but are not used to infer the infinite theorem. No hypotheses are omitted.

originality.rationale: The full initiating arXiv article establishes the n=3 equilateral specialization, not the angular profile for regular odd n>=5; it explicitly formulates an unresolved all-convex-body conjecture. Published published-finding corpus nearest claims concern symmetric-overlap area, Fraenkel asymmetry, and cut-piece diameter, none of which implies the full perimeter arc identity. Actual broad and alias searches found no stronger prior statement. Residual uninspected-source risk is recorded; a negative search is not treated as a proof of independence.

value.rationale: This determines a natural, complete all-n benchmark for the perimeter version of Winternitz splitting at the area centroid, prompted by the 2026 triangle theorem and its conjecture for general convex sets. It gives the exact directional function, a sharp odd/even symmetry dichotomy, all optimizer directions, full attainable interval, and cubic approach to half-perimeter splitting. These results are about a canonical geometric family and motivated partition observable, not an arbitrary artificial parameter slice. The n=3 case and the even-n symmetry case are acknowledged as known; value resides in the all-odd-n law and equality classification.
